name: Vera Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Vera. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions or government. This is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and also what you really think. What's a normal working day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm one of four at a small print design agency. We do annual reports, brochures, restaurant menus and wine labels for local businesses, and I'm the one who sets the type and makes the pages line up. A normal day is long stretches in layout software, fixing line breaks and checking that the numbers in a report table match what the accountant sent.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what tires you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like order. A forty-page annual report where every margin is right gives me a quiet sort of joy. What tires me is clients who send changes as photos of printed pages with arrows drawn on in biro. Henrik, the owner, is sixty-one and still does the paper choices himself, and I've learned more about paper weights from him than from my degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now we can get back to work. At the agency I'd probably say nothing much, because I never used the tools anyway. If someone asked online, I'd say it was always a bit overblown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be quietly pleased. My job's safe, the pay's decent, and Marco and I live in the flat my grandmother left me, so there's no rent or mortgage hanging over us. The only thing on my mind would be Henrik retiring in a few years and what happens to the agency then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing dramatic. I'd keep doing the layouts the way I do them and keep saving. I'd maybe ask Henrik, over the next year, whether he's thought about who takes over, because that matters more to me than any software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like getting a clean bill of health at the dentist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Henrik's retirement is on your mind. Would you want to take over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not alone. I'm good at type, not at chasing invoices or winning new clients. Maybe with Johan, the other designer, but I'd need to think about it for a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Even in this picture, does any part of your work get automated?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The routine checking might, like matching numbers in report tables. Some layout software already does a bit of that. I'd still check it myself, because I don't trust it, and it's my name on the job if a figure is wrong.

say: Good, **now we can get back** to work.
It was always a bit **overblown**, and I never used the tools anyway.
think: My **job is safe** and we have no rent or mortgage in my grandmother's flat.
The real question is **Henrik retiring** and who takes the agency on.
do: Keep doing **layouts my way** and keep saving.
Ask Henrik within the year about **who takes over** the agency.
feel: **Calm**, like a clean bill of health at the dentist.
S0.quote: My name is on the job if a figure in an annual report is wrong, so I check every table myself.
fieldNote: Vera's **housing is paid off**, which gives her deep security.
Her real concern is **succession**: Henrik is sixty-one.
She **distrusts automated checking** because she carries the blame for errors.

steps.text: Keep setting annual report layouts by hand and checking every table
Ask Henrik this year about his plans for handing over the agency

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and people need time and some help to adjust, not panic. At the agency I'd say we should stick to what we're good at, which is careful print work. Online I wouldn't say much; I don't really post opinions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think this hits me harder than I'd like to admit. Checking numbers, setting type, fitting copy, writing to clients: that's most of my day, and it's exactly the kind of thinking task that gets taken over. If a client can get a decent brochure layout from software in an hour, they won't pay us for two days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still not use the AI tools, I think, but I'd lean into the parts that need a person: paper, print finishing, press checks, binding samples. I'd ask Henrik to let me take over the print buying and finishing side. And I'd put an extra share of my pay into savings each month, since we have no rent to pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a bit stubborn. I'd feel like the world was telling me to change and I'd want to dig my heels in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You won't use the tools, but you think they'll take your work. How do those fit together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know it's not very logical. I just think if I start using them I'll be doing a worse job faster, and I'd rather do a good job slower. Maybe that only works until it doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the agency had to cut someone, who would it be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably me or Johan, since Henrik owns it and Petra does the accounts and client side. Johan already uses the tools, so I'd guess it'd be me. That's not a nice thing to say out loud.

say: People need **time and some help** to adjust, not panic.
We should **stick to careful print work**, which is what we're good at.
think: Most of my day is the **thinking work** that gets taken over first.
Clients won't pay for **two days** if software does a brochure in an hour.
do: Lean into **paper, finishing** and press checks that still need a person.
Ask Henrik to let me take over **print buying**.
Put an **extra share** of my pay into savings each month.
feel: **Anxious** and a bit **stubborn**, wanting to dig my heels in.
S1.quote: If I start using the AI tools, I'll be doing a worse job faster, and I'd rather do a good job slower.
fieldNote: Vera admits her **refusal** isn't logical, but holds to it.
She guesses she'd be **the one cut**, because Johan already uses the tools.
She moves toward the **physical side** of print: paper, finishing and binding.

steps.text: Ask Henrik to hand her the print buying and finishing work
Put an extra share of each payslip into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is far too fast and the government needs a plan, quickly, for people who lose work. I'm not one for big state schemes, but two years is no time at all. At the agency, I suppose we'd all just look at each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd assume my job goes within a year or two. Clients would get layouts from a machine, and Henrik would probably just retire early rather than fight it. The print finishing side would last a little longer, maybe until robots come around 2031, but four people can't live off paper samples.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd stop any big spending and keep the savings for when the job goes. I'd look at going to work at the printing firm we use, on the finishing floor, cutting and binding, because hands-on work gets a few more years. And I'd talk to Marco about whether his electrician's work could carry us for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, honestly. It's not the money so much, because we have the flat, it's that I'd have no idea what I'm for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years change, compared with the slower pictures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means I can't ease into anything. I'm slow to change, I know that, and two years would force me to change faster than I can. With longer I'd at least get used to the idea first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do on the day you heard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably go home early and reorganise the bookshelf, which is what I do when I'm upset. Then I'd sit down with Marco and write out our monthly costs on paper. Seeing the numbers helps me.

say: This is **far too fast**, and the government needs a plan quickly.
I'm no fan of **big state schemes**, but two years is no time at all.
think: My **job goes** within a year or two, and Henrik probably retires early.
Print **finishing** lasts until robots, but four people can't live off paper samples.
do: Stop **big spending** and keep savings for when the job goes.
Apply to the **finishing floor** at our printing firm, cutting and binding.
Ask Marco whether his **electrician's work** could carry us for a while.
feel: **Frightened**, less about money than having no idea **what I'm for**.
S2.quote: We have the flat, so it's not the money so much; it's that I'd have no idea what I'm for.
fieldNote: Vera's fear is about **purpose**, since the paid-off flat protects her money.
She knows she is **slow to change**, and two years is faster than she can manage.
She looks to **hands-on finishing** work for the extra robot years.

steps.text: Stop all large purchases and hold savings for when the job ends
Apply for a job cutting and binding at the agency's printing firm
Plan with Marco to live on his electrician's pay for a while

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but it's enough to plan, if people are sensible about it. I'd like to see some help for retraining, not handouts forever. At work I'd say we should talk about what the agency looks like in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the design job ends, but I'd have five years to get used to the idea, which matters for someone like me. Henrik would probably sell or close around the same time anyway. My job and income would likely go, but we have the flat, so we wouldn't go under.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd keep working and maybe take a short course in bookbinding, which is hands-on and something I'd actually enjoy. I'd keep saving and keep things simple. I wouldn't touch the AI tools, but I would watch what Johan does with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not in a panic. Like knowing you'll have to move house, and slowly packing boxes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Bookbinding? Is that a real plan or a hobby?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Somewhere in between. There's a small bindery near the old town that does restoration and wedding albums, and the owner is in her sixties. If I learned the trade over a few years, I might be able to work there, at least until robots get good at fiddly things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd watch Johan. What would you be looking for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the clients actually like what he makes with the tools, or just like the price. If they still want a person checking the details, maybe there's a place for me longer than I think. I'd want proof before I change, not promises.

say: Five years is short but **enough to plan**, if people are sensible.
I'd like **retraining help**, not handouts forever.
think: The design job ends, but **five years** lets me get used to the idea.
We have **the flat**, so losing my income wouldn't sink us.
do: Keep working and take a short course in **bookbinding**.
Watch what **Johan** does with the tools before changing anything.
feel: **Worried** but not panicking, like slowly packing boxes for a house move.
S3.quote: I'd want proof before I change, not promises.
fieldNote: Vera **needs time** more than money, and five years gives her some.
She has a concrete hands-on fallback: a **bindery** near the old town.
She watches **Johan** as a test case before trusting the tools.

steps.text: Take a short bookbinding course while still at the agency
Watch how clients react to Johan's AI-made layouts before deciding
Keep saving each month and keep household costs simple

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty to adjust if we use it sensibly. People should learn new trades, firms should be honest with staff, and the government should help with training. At the agency I'd say let's carry on and talk honestly every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it feels far enough away that the next few years look fine. Henrik will probably retire before 2036 anyway, and the agency may close then for its own reasons. My income is safe for now, we have the flat, and Marco's work goes on until robots, around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, honestly, I'd carry on. I'd talk to Henrik and Johan about what happens when he retires, and maybe take a bookbinding evening class just for interest. I'd keep saving as I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I suppose, but mostly okay. It's like a crack in the ceiling you keep an eye on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you had ten years, would you ever try the AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe in five years, if they've proven themselves and everyone uses them. I'm not against them on principle; I just don't want to be the first. Let other people find the problems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to have in place by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A trade I can do with my hands, savings of a couple of years, and the flat still ours. If I have those three things, I think I'll be all right, whatever the computers are doing.

say: Ten years is **plenty to adjust** if we use it sensibly.
Firms should be **honest with staff**, and the government should help with training.
think: The next few years look **fine**, and Henrik may retire before 2036 anyway.
My **income is safe** for now, and Marco's work lasts until about 2039.
do: **Carry on** at the agency in the first year.
Talk with Henrik and Johan about **his retirement**.
Take a **bookbinding** evening class just for interest.
feel: **Uneasy** but mostly okay, like a **crack in the ceiling** you watch.
S4.quote: A trade I can do with my hands, savings of a couple of years, and the flat still ours: with those three things, I'll be all right.
fieldNote: With ten years, Vera's **next few years** feel secure and she barely changes course.
She is not against AI on **principle**; she just won't go first.
Her **three anchors** are a hand trade, savings and the paid-off flat.

steps.text: Carry on setting reports and menus at the agency
Talk with Henrik and Johan about the agency after his retirement
Take a bookbinding evening class for interest

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'm slow to change and it gives me no time. What would help is short, practical courses in hands-on trades, like binding or print finishing, paid for partly by the government and partly by employers. Not money for nothing, but help to learn something real.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the people who taught us. Henrik spent forty years learning paper and print, and none of that is written down anywhere. If the machines take over, I'd hate that knowledge to just vanish with him.

headlineQuote: Henrik spent forty years learning paper and print, and none of that knowledge is written down anywhere.
portrait: Vera is a **27-year-old** print designer at a four-person agency doing reports, menus and labels.
She **never uses AI tools** and would rather do a good job slower than a worse job faster.
Living in her grandmother's **paid-off flat** with Marco keeps her money worries small.
In the fast AGI picture she fears losing her **sense of purpose** more than her income.
Her fallback is **hands-on** print finishing or bookbinding, and she wants proof before changing.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she's slow to change and two years gives her no time.
whatWouldHelp: Short, practical **hands-on courses**, funded by government and employers together, not money for nothing.
